query: Reported superconducting high-entropy alloys are dominated by Nb-Ta matrices, while other studies concern titanium-rich systems based on heavy transition metals and partly ordered systems. Consequently, these precedents do not establish what controls superconductivity in high-entropy alloys outside the best-studied material classes. Within the defining constraint of a solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each, what governs superconducting behavior in such an uncharacterized high-entropy alloy, and why? State one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison against the starting material, predicted observations relative to the baseline, applicable boundary conditions, the earlier evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In a single‐phase, disordered bcc high‐entropy alloy that meets the criterion of containing at least five elements at no less than the minimum required atomic percent each, the superconducting transition temperature is governed by the degree of local lattice distortion—specifically, the severe lattice distortion characteristic of multi‐principal element systems caused by atomic size mismatch—which modifies the phonon spectrum and strengthens electron–phonon coupling, thereby raising Tc relative to Nb–Ta‐dominated HEAs.
generation.material_initial_state: A well‐characterized Nb–Ta‐dominated HEA (e.g., (TaNb)0.67(HfZrTi)0.33) with a single-phase body‐centered cubic (bcc) solid solution and a reported Tc of ~7.7 K at ambient pressure.
generation.intervention: Substitute a portion of Nb and/or Ta with additional titanium while maintaining at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each, ensuring that the alloy remains a single-phase, disordered bcc solid solution.
generation.conditions: Synthesis and processing conditions that preserve a homogeneous single-phase bcc structure at ambient pressure, with superconducting properties measured via resistivity, magnetic susceptibility, and specific heat at low temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced local lattice distortions, evidenced by broadened XRD peaks and local structure probes such as TEM or pair distribution function analysis, which alter the phonon spectrum and electron–phonon coupling.
generation.mechanism: Increasing the titanium content introduces a greater mismatch in atomic radii, which in a multi-principal element system results in severe lattice distortion; this softens certain phonon modes and strengthens the electron–phonon coupling, ultimately leading to an enhanced superconducting transition temperature.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline Nb–Ta-dominated HEA, the Ti-enhanced alloy will exhibit a moderately higher Tc (potentially several tenths of a Kelvin increase) and possibly altered upper critical field values, accompanied by measurable increases in lattice distortion parameters.
generation.baseline: The baseline HEA, such as (TaNb)0.67(HfZrTi)0.33, which shows robust superconductivity with Tc ≈ 7.7–7.8 K and minimal pressure sensitivity.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold as long as the alloy remains a homogeneous single-phase bcc solid solution; if excessive Ti causes phase separation or ordering (e.g., formation of a secondary hcp phase like in Sc additions), the hypothesis may no longer apply. Also, the overall valence electron count should remain in a range similar to that of the baseline to avoid confounding effects.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative change in Tc and the competing influences of electronic density of states versus phonon softening remain uncertain until measured. There is also uncertainty regarding the limits of Ti substitution before phase stability is compromised.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of HEA samples with gradually increasing Ti content by partially replacing Nb and/or Ta while keeping the overall composition within the single-phase bcc region and maintaining all elements at or above 5 at.%. Characterize the crystal structure with XRD and TEM to ensure homogeneity, and measure superconducting properties (Tc, upper critical field) via resistivity and susceptibility measurements at low temperatures. Additionally, employ local structure analysis (such as pair distribution function or high-resolution TEM) to quantify lattice distortions.
measurements: XRD peak broadening and lattice parameter changes
TEM and pair distribution function analyses for local strain
Resistivity vs. temperature to determine Tc
Magnetic susceptibility and specific heat measurements to confirm superconductivity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If increasing the Ti content under conditions that preserve a single-phase bcc structure does not lead to a systematic correlation between increased local lattice distortions and a higher Tc (i.e., if Tc remains statistically indistinguishable from that of the baseline, or even decreases), then the hypothesis that lattice distortion-driven modulation of electron–phonon coupling controls superconductivity in these HEAs is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In 2014, the first superconducting high-entropy alloy Ta0.34Nb0.33Hf0.08Zr0.14Ti0.11 (in at.%) was discovered []. According to Sun and Cava [], this alloy can be classified as a type-A HEA superconductor. HEAs of this type contain only metals on the left side of the transition metal region of the periodic table, crystallize in a body-centered cubic (bcc) lattice, and exhibit superconducting transition temperatures (Tc) between 4.0 and 9.2 K, while their highest upper critical field (μ0Hc2) is close to 12 T [,,,,,,]. These are the most widely studied HEA superconductors to date. However, it should be noted that most of these alloys contain a large amount of niobium and tantalum, while the titanium concentration is typically less than 20 at.%. Because binary Nb-Ti alloys exhibit much better superconducting properties than Nb-Ta [], it is plausible to expect that NbTi-based high-entropy alloys will have a higher Tc and/or μ0Hc2 compared to previously reported type-A HEA superconductors. Moreover, in the case of various ternary Nb-Ti-Hf and Nb-Ti-Ta and quaternary Nb-Ti-Ta-Hf alloys, the highest values of μ0Hc2 were observed for the titanium-rich alloys []. Pressure is one of the variables that can uncover unexpected phenomena and properties (). For superconductors in particular, the pressure-induced enhancement of critical transition temperatures in copper-oxide and iron-pnictide superconductors (), the reemergence of superconductivity in the alkaline iron selenide () and heavy fermion superconductors (), pressure-induced superconductivity in H3S () and elements (, ), are examples. Therefore, looking for new phenomena in the superconducting HEA under pressure is of great interest. Here we report high-pressure studies on the superconducting HEA (TaNb)0.67(HfZrTi)0.33, which has a critical transition temperature to the superconducting state (TC) of about 7.8 K at ambient pressure (, ). Our observations demonstrate that this alloy exhibits extraordinarily robust superconductivity––its zero-resistance superconducting state is still achieved even at a pressure of 190.6 GPa, or almost 2 megabars (1 Mbar = 1011 pascal), a pressure like that within the outer core of the earth. Such a superconductor with a highly robust zero-resistance state, existing continuously from 1 atm to geological pressures, is extremely unusual and is in fact unique

cited_evidence.text: The Sc-Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr system comprises five superconducting (SC) elements Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti and Zr, all belonging to the class of low-temperature superconductors, whereas Sc is non-superconducting at ambient pressure. The SC transition temperatures TC of pure metals are collected in Table 4, ranging from the highest TCNb= 9.20 K to the lowest TCHf= 0.12 K. We have studied the SC transition via electrical resistivity, specific heat and the Meissner effect. The experimental details are described in the Methods Section.

The addition of scandium has a detrimental effect on both the single-phase character of the Sc-Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys and the homogeneity of their microstructure. Scandium is responsible for the appearance of the hcp phase fraction, which absorbs more or less all Sc, but is poor in Ta and Nb. The resulting two-phase structure is highly inhomogeneous. Large Ta- and Nb-rich, but Sc-poor bcc dendrites (or islands) of several 10 to 100 µm cross dimension are formed, which are quite homogeneous in the interior, but become a fine dispersion of sub-micron precipitates of the bcc and hcp phases close to the edges. A similar fine dispersion of the sub-micron bcc and hcp precipitates (where the latter are in majority) is also characteristic of the interdendritic regions, which do not contain any large, µm-size hcp regions. Superconductivity of the Sc-Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr system is closely related to the parent Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr system.
